opus-5.5.text:
I usually break generalization into a few layers, because "it generalizes" can mean very different things.

The first layer is **visual or environmental generalization**: same task, same objects, but different lighting, backgrounds, camera angles, table textures. This is the easiest to get, and pretrained vision backbones and diverse data collection take you quite far. If a model fails here, it's usually a data coverage problem rather than a deep modeling problem.

The second layer is **object generalization**: can it pick up a cup it has never seen, with a different shape, material, or weight? This is harder because it touches physical properties, not just appearance. A transparent or deformable object behaves very differently from a rigid opaque one, even if they look semantically similar.

The third layer is **task or instruction generalization**: can it compose skills it already has into something new, or follow an instruction phrased in a way it hasn't encountered? This is where language and world knowledge from large pretrained models really help. We see some promising signs, but I'd be honest that it's still far from robust. The model often understands what you want but can't reliably execute the motion.

The fourth, and hardest, is **embodiment generalization**: transferring across different robot arms, grippers, or even mobile bases. The action spaces, kinematics, and dynamics all change. This is the one I think matters most long term, because if every new robot needs its own dataset from scratch, the field doesn't scale.

How do we assess it? Mostly by deliberately holding out one dimension at a time: unseen scenes, unseen objects, unseen instructions, unseen embodiments. Then we look at success rates on real hardware, not just simulation, because sim results can be misleading. Beyond the success rate, we also look at *how* it fails. A model that fails gracefully, retries, or recovers is telling you something different from one that just freezes.

If I'm candid, the current state is: decent on the first layer, partial on the second, early on the third, and the fourth is still largely an open research question. That's what makes it exciting.

r001.rationale: It mentions retries and recovery as ways to assess failures, but does not identify handling unexpected situations during execution as a generalization dimension.

r002.rationale: It rates environmental generalization as relatively strong and task generalization as weak, but does not specifically assess positional generalization.

r003.rationale: It says task recombination is not robust, but does not attribute that difficulty to insufficient task diversity in robot training data.

fable-5.1.text:
When we talk about generalization in robotics, I think it's dangerous to treat it as a single number. Internally we break it into several dimensions, and we evaluate each one separately, because a model can look very strong on one and be almost useless on another.

The first dimension is visual or environmental generalization. Does the model still work when you change the lighting, the background, the tabletop, the distractor objects? This is the easiest one to make progress on, mostly because it is where vision foundation models and large-scale pretraining already help us a lot. If you give the model enough diversity in what it sees, it becomes fairly robust here.

The second is object generalization. You train on a certain set of cups and bottles, and then you hand it a cup it has never seen, with a different shape, different material, different weight. This is harder, because now the model needs an implicit understanding of physical properties, not just appearance. A transparent glass and a ceramic mug look very different to a camera but should be handled similarly. We care a lot about how many object categories we can cover and how far outside the training distribution we can go before performance collapses.

The third is spatial and layout generalization. The same object, the same task, but now it's on the left instead of the right, or it's higher up, or there's a shelf in the way. This exposes whether the model has really learned something about geometry or just memorized trajectories. Honestly, this is where many imitation learning policies still fall apart, and it is a good diagnostic for us.

The fourth is task and instruction generalization. Can you compose skills? If the model has seen "pick up the cup" and "open the drawer," can it do "put the cup in the drawer" from a language instruction it has never encountered? This is the dimension that most depends on the language and reasoning side of the model, and it's where the connection to large language models becomes meaningful rather than just a buzzword.

And then there is the one I think people underestimate: embodiment generalization. Different robot arms, different grippers, different camera placements. If you collect data on one platform and the model only works on that platform, you haven't really built a general model, you've built a very expensive controller. Being able to transfer across embodiments is what will determine whether robotics data can actually scale the way text and image data did.

So when someone asks me "how general is your model," my honest answer is always: along which axis? We maintain separate benchmarks for each of these, and we track them independently. The goal is not to get a high average. The goal is to understand which dimension is the bottleneck right now, because that tells us where to put the next round of data and the next round of research effort.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changes in lighting, objects, and layout, but does not identify unexpected situations arising during task execution as a generalization dimension.

r002.rationale: It discusses spatial and task generalization separately, but does not assess the current model as better at positional generalization than at performing entirely unseen tasks.

r003.rationale: It asks whether the model can compose skills into an unseen task, but does not attribute difficulty to insufficient task diversity in robot training data.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate generalization into a few dimensions. One is visual generalization: if we change the lighting, the background, or the appearance of an object, can the robot still perform the same task? Another is spatial generalization: if we move objects around or change the initial configuration, can it adapt its actions?

Then there’s task generalization. Can it handle a new combination of skills it has already learned, or does every new task require additional demonstrations? And there’s generalization across embodiments—whether what it learns on one robot transfers to a robot with different physical characteristics.

For our current model, I’d be careful about treating these as a single capability. Success on unfamiliar objects doesn’t necessarily imply success on unfamiliar tasks. The assessment should hold out each dimension separately, then combine changes to see where performance breaks down. I’d also look beyond task success to how consistently the robot succeeds and whether it can recover when something goes wrong.

r001.rationale: The response mentions recovery when something goes wrong, but does not identify handling unexpected situations during task execution as a dimension of generalization.

r002.rationale: It discusses positional and task generalization as separate dimensions, but does not say the current model performs better on positional generalization than on entirely unseen tasks.

r003.rationale: It raises whether new combinations of learned skills require more demonstrations, but does not attribute difficulty to insufficient task diversity in the training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d break generalization down into a few dimensions. One is visual generalization: if we change the background, lighting, or the appearance of an object, can the robot still perform the task? Another is generalization to new objects—especially when their geometry or physical properties differ from what the model has seen.

Then there’s task generalization. Can the model combine familiar skills to follow a new instruction, rather than simply repeat a sequence from training? And there’s generalization across environments and robot embodiments, where the workspace, camera configuration, or hardware changes.

To assess these, I think it’s important to separate the dimensions first. Hold out objects, environments, or task combinations and test them independently, then look at what happens when several things change together. Success rate matters, but so does the type of failure: did the robot misunderstand the instruction, fail to perceive the object, or struggle with execution? That tells us much more about the limits of generalization than a single aggregate number.

r001.rationale: The response discusses visual, object, task, environment, and embodiment generalization, but does not identify handling unexpected situations during task execution as a dimension.

r002.rationale: It does not compare positional generalization with performance on entirely unseen tasks or say the model is better at the former.

r003.rationale: It mentions combining familiar skills into new tasks, but does not attribute difficulty doing so to insufficient task diversity in the robot training data.
